 Slotkin Joins Colleagues Demanding USDA Withdraw Rule Restricting Food Assistance for Michiganders   
 Sign Up For Updates 
 Nov 17, 2026 | Press Releases 
 WASHINGTON, D.C.  -— U.S. Senator Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), a member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, along with fellow committee Democrats, urged the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that will severely narrow eligibility requirements for the nation’s largest anti-hunger program.   
 This rule could potentially lead to the loss of SNAP benefits for tens of thousands of Michiganders. Over 150,000 Michiganders, including an estimated 54,000 children, have already lost access to SNAP benefits as a result of the cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.     
 “We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs,”   said the senators. 
 Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility helps working families and seniors afford groceries at a time when the rising costs of housing, child-care, health care, and other necessities are stretching household budgets. It gives states flexibility to help low-income households access food assistance while supporting work and financial stability.
 Without BBCE, families could lose SNAP benefits even when they are still struggling to make ends meet. It also allows families and seniors to build and maintain modest savings without jeopardizing their access to food assistance.  
 This proposed rule would also make SNAP more challenging and costly for states to administer, increasing paperwork, the risk of payment errors, and demands on state workers.  
 Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility could also lose automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families to submit additional applications to establish eligibility and creating more administrative work for schools.  
 This added red tape could prevent eligible children from receiving meals and reduce federal reimbursements for schools, threatening efforts to provide free school meals to all students. The proposal could also create additional red tape for families seeking assistance through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), potentially leaving some families unable to access benefits and others ineligible for assistance altogether.  
 The text of the letter is available  here .
